The applet gives you ten colours and asks for a colouring that uses as few as possible. The rule is one sentence long, but finding the very best colouring is a real puzzle.

Proper colourings

A graph colouring gives each dot, or vertex, a colour. It is proper when two vertices joined by an edge never get the same colour. The applet lets you colour any vertex any way you like, so it is up to you to keep the colouring proper. Its Total colors used: counter simply counts the different colours on coloured vertices — an uncoloured vertex is not counted.

The chromatic number

The aim on the page is to beat that counter: find a proper colouring with the fewest colours. That smallest number is the chromatic number of the graph:

chi(G) = the least k for which G has a proper k-colouring

Of the six graphs on this page, Graph 1 is a bipartite tree and needs 2 colours; Graph 2 is a wheel and needs 3; Graphs 3, 4 and 6 need 4, and Graph 5 needs 3. The logic test finds these by searching every possible colouring, so the numbers are checked rather than guessed.

Why the minimum is hard

A greedy rule — take the vertices in order and give each the first colour none of its coloured neighbours uses — always produces a proper colouring, but not always the shortest one. To be sure you have the minimum you must rule out every colouring with fewer colours. The logic test checks two different search methods against each other on all 64 graphs with four vertices, on the six samples, and on 120 randomly generated graphs.

The applet itself never computes the chromatic number; it only counts the colours you have used. The exact numbers here are worked out from the definitions printed on the applet's own page.

Try Graph 3: a greedy colouring can use five colours there, but four are enough. Can you find the four-colour one?
